title: Process cleanup must preserve the existing reaping owner
applies_when: A Python POSIX process-tree cleanup candidate adds psutil.wait_procs or os.waitpid to eliminate zombies, while callers may own multiprocessing.Process objects or another lifecycle manager.
lesson: Trace which object owns child exit status before adding a second waiter. psutil's POSIX wait consumes child status through waitpid; CPython's fork-based multiprocessing owner independently calls waitpid and caches its return code. A second reaper can remove the OS process but leave the original Process object with no exit code. Test owner-visible exitcode, join, is_alive and close after cleanup, not only absence of a zombie PID. Prefer lifecycle cleanup through the owning manager when available. A raw os.fork regression with no manager does not establish that a generic reaping patch preserves supported consumers.
avoid_when: This mechanism is scoped to competing POSIX child reapers, not every Windows handle or async process API. A helper that exclusively owns raw children may legitimately reap them. Establish actual callers before claiming application impact or selecting a repair. The linked implementations explain the mechanism, not a particular framework's CI failures, native test result or performance.

evidence.note: The POSIX wait wrapper consumes exit status with os.waitpid; the pidfd termination path subsequently invokes this wrapper.
The fork Popen owner caches returncode only after its own waitpid succeeds; OSError instead leaves poll returning None. This supports the ownership countercondition.
The public lifecycle contract includes exitcode, join, is_alive and close; close rejects an object considered still running.
